The East Amazonian fire-eye (Pyriglena leuconota) is a medium-sized antbird inhabiting the understory of lowland terra firme forests, where its life history traits reflect the energetic constraints of a relatively stable tropical environment. Neonates emerge from eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] and weigh approximately 4.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.3 grams] at hatching, a modest birth mass that is comparable to values reported for the related bare-eyed antbird Rhegmatorhina melanosticta from similar Amazonian habitats. This initial mass is quickly augmented through intensive biparental provisioning, as the altricial nestlings require substantial food delivery to support rapid feather development and thermoregulatory competence. The incubation period itself, which determines the age at which the chick breaks free of the eggshell, lasts approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] at these incubation temperatures, a duration that is typical for thamnophilid antbirds of at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]this body size.

Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic period, maintained at approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], several key developmental and reproductive milestones have been documented in field studies. Fledging, the point at which the young bird leaves the nest and achieves its first sustained flight, occurs quite rapidly, with nestlings departing the nest at about 10.5 days after hatching [tx = about 10.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This early fledging age is characteristic of many small to medium-sized insectivorous passerines and is likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk during the nestling stage, despite the trade-off of requiring a prolonged period of post-fledging parental care. Following fledging, the young birds undergo a period of growth and behavioral maturation as independent foraging skills are gradually acquired in dense understory vegetation, a process that extends well beyond the initial nest departure and requires several additional weeks of guided parental assistance before full independence is achieved.

Sexual maturity, defined as the age at which the gonads become fully functional and capable of gamete production, is reached considerably later in the developmental schedule of this antbird. At 32 days after hatching [tp = 32 days after hatching], under the same warm thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], puberty marks the physiological onset of reproductive capacity — a relatively rapid maturation to puberty when compared to many temperate-zone passerines, consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes early investment in reproduction. The timing of gonadal activation allows the individual to complete somatic growth while already possessing the physiological machinery for reproduction, a pattern that may be favored in aseasonal tropical environments where mild conditions prevail year-round and food resources remain sufficiently predictable to support early maturation.

The age at which a female produces her first successful brood is a critical demographic parameter, and for this species it occurs at approximately 547 days after hatching [tR = approximately 547 days after hatching] when active body temperatures average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This prolonged delay between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction is presumably linked to the time required for territory establishment, pair-bond formation, and the acquisition of sufficient foraging experience to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The reproductive output itself involves females laying 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a modal clutch size that is consistent throughout the Thamnophilidae. Pairs may attempt up to 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = up to 2 clutches each year], resulting in a maximum annual reproductive output that is constrained by the length of the breeding season and the need to balance repeated nesting attempts with molt and survival, a trade-off common among Neotropical passerines.

The maximum lifespan of this species has been estimated at 3,467 days [am = 3,467 days] under field conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a longevity that is notable among Neotropical passerines of comparable mass. This extended lifespan is likely facilitated by a relatively low daily metabolic ceiling; basal oxygen consumption measured in resting birds reaches 100 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 100 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reflecting a standard metabolic rate that is modest for an antbird of this size. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females is around 32.3 grams [Wwi = around 32.3 grams], falling within the broader published range of 26 to 36 grams for the species. This moderate adult mass, combined with a low metabolic intensity and a slow-paced reproductive schedule, underscores a life history strategy that emphasizes survival and iteroparity over high fecundity — an adaptive suite characteristic of many understory insectivores in stable tropical ecosystems that face high annual survivorship and limited seasonal variation in resource availability.
